mainTopic: Assessing a person's value (דמים) versus fixed ערכין: heirs, body parts, 'half' pledges, and pledges on vessels.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a chain of questions about pledging one's own market value (דמים): two separate pledges, one pledge of 'twice my value', and an assessment the court made on its own. A proof from a משנה about a person who pledged his value and died is brought and then pushed off, so that question stays unresolved. Then a new משנה teaches that ערכין are stricter than דמים in one way: heirs pay a ערך after the pledger dies, but not דמים, because the dead have no value. The משנה also covers pledging the ערך of a limb, of a vital organ, of 'half my ערך' versus 'the ערך of half of me', and of another person's value. The גמרא explains that heirs pay a ערך only when the pledger stood in judgment, while דמים still needs an assessment. It brings רב's ruling that pledging a limb's ערך obligates its value according to רבי מאיר. It gives the פסוק sources for the vital-organ rule for both ערכין and דמים, and explains רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's 'lashes' as a rabbinic penalty. Finally, אביי and רבא explain why the חכמים void a pledge of half a כלי's ערך, and the גמרא shows why the משנה repeats its clause about another person's value.

steps.title: Two separate value pledges: one assessment or two?
steps.stepSummary: A person said "דמי עלי" and then said it again. The question is whether we assess his value one time and he pays double, or whether we assess him separately for each pledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we assess him one time? Or perhaps, since he made his vows one after the other, we assess him two times?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a question that started just before this text. A man pledged his own value twice, one pledge after the other. It asks how many times we must assess his value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With דמים, the payment is not a fixed sum. It is his real worth, judged the way a slave's price would be judged, and that worth can change over time. If the two vows count as one obligation, one assessment is enough and he pays it twice. If each vow is its own obligation, each one may need its own assessment, made at its own time.

keyTerms.meaning: "My value is upon me": a pledge to give the Temple his actual market worth
We assess (estimate how much he is worth)
One after the other (sequentially)
Or perhaps: introduces the second side of a question

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up דמים with ערכין. ערך is a fixed amount set by the תורה according to age and gender. דמים is the person's actual market value, so it needs an assessment.

phrases.english: Do we assess him one time,
phrases.notes: This finishes a question that began just before this text, about someone who said "דמי עלי" twice.

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether two separate value pledges need one assessment or two.

steps.title: Saying "twice my value" in one statement
steps.stepSummary: Suppose separate vows do need two assessments. What about someone who said "שני דמי עלי" (twice my value) all at once?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that since he vowed one after the other we assess him twice, what if he said "twice my value is upon me" all at once? Here he surely vowed at one time, so we assess him once. Or perhaps, since he said "twice," it is like vowing one after the other?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא builds a second question on top of the first. It assumes the first answer is "two assessments." Then it asks whether that answer also applies when the double pledge was made in one sentence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to look at it. He spoke only once, which suggests one assessment. But the word "twice" splits the pledge into two units, which may make it like two separate vows. The question is whether we follow the single moment of speaking or the double content of what he said.

keyTerms.meaning: "And if you say": assume one answer, then ask a further question
At one time (in a single statement)
What is the law?
Twice my value

phrases.english: And if you say:
since he vowed one after the other,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: ״שְׁנֵי דָּמַי עָלַי״ בְּבַת אַחַת, מַהוּ?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the assumed answer to step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a single statement of "twice my value" counts as one vow or as two sequential vows.

steps.title: Someone already assessed for another reason
steps.stepSummary: Suppose "twice" does count as two vows. What if a court had already assessed him on its own, not for the vow? Does that earlier assessment count?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that since he said "twice" it is like one after the other, what if they assessed him on their own? Do we say he already stands assessed? Or perhaps the assessment must be done with intent for this purpose?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a third question to the chain. It asks whether an assessment that was done for some unrelated reason can count for his vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One view says the facts are already known: his value has been determined, so there is no reason to do it again. The other view says the assessment is part of the process of הקדש, so it must be done with intent (כוונה) for that purpose. The question is whether the assessment only reveals information or is a formal legal act.

keyTerms.meaning: They assessed him on their own (not for the sake of the vow)
He already stands assessed
Intent
Assessment (estimate of value)

steps.whyThisMatters: This raises a common question in הלכה: is a procedure just a way of finding out a fact, or must it be done with intent to count?

steps.whatToRemember: There are three questions, and each one stands on the one before it: (1) two vows, one after the other; (2) "twice" said all at once; (3) an assessment done without intent.

steps.title: Starting to resolve one question from a משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer at least one of the questions. It quotes a משנה: if someone pledged his value and died, his heirs do not pay, because the dead have no value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Resolve at least one of them, as we learned: if someone said "my value is upon me" and died, the heirs do not give, because there is no value for the dead.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a proof by quoting a משנה. It explains how the משנה proves the point in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches that once he dies, there is no way to assess him. So the heirs pay nothing, even though he had made a pledge. This suggests that the obligation depends on an assessment of him, and the גמרא is about to use that idea to settle one of the questions.

keyTerms.meaning: Resolve (answer the question)
At least one
Heirs
The dead have no monetary value

phrases.english: Resolve at least one,

the heirs do not give,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to resolve one of the three questions.
steps.raayaObject: At least one of the three questions about assessment.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: someone who pledged his value and died; his heirs do not pay, because there is no value for the dead.

steps.title: Everyone is worth at least four זוזים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the proof from the משנה. If an assessment made on its own counted, then every person would already count as assessed at a minimum of four זוזים. So the heirs should have to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think an assessment made on its own counts, then this man is already 'assessed.' Is there any man who is not worth four זוזים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the משנה from the last step answers the question about an assessment the court made on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If any assessment counts, even one not made for the vow, then the obvious fact that every person is worth at least four זוזים should count too. The heirs would then have to pay at least that much. Since the משנה says the heirs pay nothing, the conclusion is that the assessment must be done for the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: They assessed him on their own, not because of a vow
An assessment of a person's worth
He already stands assessed
זוזים, silver coins

phrases.english: And if it enters your mind

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the משנה quoted in step 4 answers the question from step 3
steps.raayaObject: That an assessment made on its own does not count for a vow
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה that heirs do not pay for 'דמי עלי' after the person dies

steps.title: A real assessment is different from none at all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. When a court assessed him on its own, a real assessment took place. In the משנה's case, no assessment ever happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they assessed him on their own, he really went through an assessment. When he said 'my value is upon me' and died, he never went through an assessment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from the last step and shows that the משנה does not answer the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being 'obviously worth four זוזים' is not the same as an actual court assessment. In the case of the question, a court really did assess him. So the משנה, where no one assessed him at all, tells us nothing about that case, and the question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: He actually went through an assessment
'My value is upon me': a vow to give one's market value

steps.confusionAlert: This rejection does not decide that an assessment made on its own does count. It only shows that the משנה cannot prove either side.

phrases.english: When they assessed him on their own

he never went into an assessment

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 5
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the משנה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's case had no actual assessment, unlike a case where a court really assessed him on its own

steps.title: Valuations are stricter than vows of value
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה teaches that if someone pledges his ערך and dies, his heirs must pay. But if he pledges his דמים and dies, they do not pay, because the dead have no value.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Valuations are stricter than vows. How so? If someone says 'my valuation is upon me' and dies, the heirs must give. If he says 'my value is upon me' and dies, the heirs do not give, because the dead have no value.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It compares a vow of ערך with a vow of דמים when the person dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערך is a fixed amount set by the תורה based on age and gender, so it is known the moment he makes the vow. It becomes a debt that his heirs must pay. A vow of דמים depends on his worth, and after death he has no worth, so there is nothing to collect.

keyTerms.meaning: A stringency, a way one law is stricter
Fixed valuations set by the תורה
'My valuation is upon me': a vow to give one's fixed ערך
Heirs
The dead have no monetary value

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the same משנה the גמרא used in its proof. Here it appears in its own place, at the start of a new משנה.

phrases.english: MISHNAH
There is a stringency in valuations over vows
phrases.notes: 'Vows' here means vows to give your market value (דמים).

phrases.english: How so?
One who says, 'My valuation is upon me,' and dies
the heirs must give

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Heirs pay a ערך pledged before death, but not a pledge of value (דמים)

steps.title: Pledging the valuation of a body part
steps.stepSummary: If someone pledges the ערך of his hand or leg, his words mean nothing. If he pledges the ערך of a body part that life depends on, like the head or liver, he gives his whole ערך.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The valuation of my hand' or 'the valuation of my leg is upon me' means nothing. 'The valuation of my head' or 'the valuation of my liver is upon me' means he gives the valuation of his whole self. The rule is: for a part that life depends on, he gives the valuation of his whole self.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a new case: pledging the ערך of only one part of the body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה gives a ערך only for a whole person, so a hand or leg has no ערך of its own. A body part that a person cannot live without counts as the whole person. That is why pledging its ערך means pledging his full ערך.

keyTerms.meaning: He has said nothing; the vow has no effect
My liver
The valuation of his whole self
This is the general rule
Life depends on it

steps.whatToRemember: A ערך exists only for a whole person. A limb life does not depend on counts for nothing. A part life depends on counts as the whole person.

phrases.english: 'The valuation of my hand,' or 'The valuation of my leg is upon me'
he has said nothing
'The valuation of my head,' or 'The valuation of my liver is upon me'

steps.triggerLanguage: עֵרֶךְ יָדִי וְעֵרֶךְ רַגְלִי עָלַי לָא אָמַר כְּלוּם

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pledging the ערך of a limb life does not depend on has no effect. Pledging the ערך of a part life depends on obligates the full ערך.

steps.title: Half of my value versus the value of half of me
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that 'half my ערך' means paying half, but 'the ערך of half of me' means paying the whole ערך. The same applies to דמים. The rule: pledging a part that life depends on obligates the whole amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'Half my ערך is upon me,' he gives half his ערך. If he says 'The ערך of half of me is upon me,' he gives his whole ערך. If he says 'Half my דמים is upon me,' he gives half his worth. If he says 'The דמים of half of me is upon me,' he gives his whole worth. This is the rule: if he pledged a part that the soul depends on, he gives the worth of his whole self.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues from step 8 and gives four cases of pledging 'half'. It then sums them up with a general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Half my ערך' splits the money, so he pays half. 'The ערך of half of me' points to half of his body, and nobody can live without half his body. So, like the head or liver in step 8, it counts as pledging his whole self. The closing rule says this outright: any part that life depends on obligates the full amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Half of my ערך: half of the money amount
The ערך of half of me: the value of half of my body
A person's market worth (what he would sell for as a slave)
This is the general rule
A body part that life depends on

steps.confusionAlert: The words look almost the same, but the order changes everything. 'חֲצִי עֶרְכִּי' (half of my value) means paying half. 'עֵרֶךְ חֶצְיִי' (the value of half of me) means paying the whole amount.

phrases.english: "Half my valuation is upon me" —
he gives half his valuation.
"The valuation of half of me is upon me" —
he gives the valuation of his whole self.
"Half my worth is upon me" —
he gives half his worth.
"The worth of half of me is upon me" —
he gives the worth of his whole self.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends step 8's rule about vital body parts to the case of 'half', and adds a general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Half my ערך/דמים' means paying half. 'ערך/דמים of half of me' means paying the full amount, because life depends on that part.

steps.title: Pledging someone else's value when someone dies
steps.stepSummary: If someone pledges another person's ערך and both die, the pledger's heirs pay. For דמים, the heirs pay if the pledger dies, but not if the person whose worth was pledged dies, because the dead have no worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'The ערך of so-and-so is upon me,' and both the pledger and that person die, the heirs pay. If he says 'The דמים of so-and-so is upon me,' and the pledger dies, the heirs pay. If the person whose worth was pledged dies, the heirs do not pay, because the dead have no worth.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה takes the death rule from step 7 and applies it to pledging another person's value. It separates two cases: the pledger dies, or the pledged person dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערך is a fixed amount that became a debt the moment the vow was made. So even if both people die, the pledger's estate still owes it. דמים depends on the pledged person's actual worth. If that person dies, there is no worth left to pay. If only the pledger dies, the debt passes to his heirs.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so; some other person
The one who made the vow
The person whose value was pledged
Heirs, who pay debts out of the estate
The dead have no market worth

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows what really matters for דמים: whether the pledged person is alive. The pledger's own death does not matter, because his debt simply passes to his estate.

phrases.english: One who says: "The valuation of so-and-so is upon me,"
and the one who vowed and the one vowed about die —
the heirs must give.
"The worth of so-and-so is upon me,"
and the one who vowed dies — the heirs must give;
if the one vowed about dies — the heirs do not give,
because the dead have no worth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies step 7's death rule to pledging another person's value.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For another person's ערך, the heirs always pay. For another person's דמים, the heirs pay only if the pledger dies, not if the pledged person dies.

steps.title: Ways vows of worth are stricter than ערכין
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches two ways נדרים are stricter than ערכין. Vows of worth apply to animals and birds, and they are not reduced for a poor person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: נדרים are stricter than ערכין in some ways. Vows of worth take effect on cattle, wild animals, and birds. Also, they are not judged by what the person can afford. This is not so with ערכין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by quoting a ברייתא that compares vows of worth with ערכין. This first half lists where vows of worth are stricter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ערכין apply only to people, and a poor person pays only what he can afford. A vow of worth, by contrast, can be made about an animal or a bird, which must then be valued and paid. A poor person who vows worth also owes the full amount, with no reduction.

keyTerms.meaning: A stricter side, a way one law is harsher
Here: vows to give the market worth of something
Cattle, wild animals, and birds
What a person can afford; a poor person pays less in ערכין

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
There is a stricter side to vows than to valuations,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהַנְּדָרִים חָלִין עַל בְּהֵמָה חַיָּה וָעוֹף,
phrases.english: for vows take effect on cattle, wild animals, and birds,
and they are not judged by what one can afford,
phrases.notes: In ערכין, a poor person pays only what he can afford (ויקרא 27:8). A vow of value gets no such break.

phrases.english: which is not so with valuations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא begins with a ברייתא that compares the two kinds of vows the משנה has been discussing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vows of worth apply to animals and birds and are not reduced for a poor person. ערכין are different on both points.

steps.title: The one way ערכין are stricter than vows of worth
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. ערכין are stricter in one way: if the pledger dies, his heirs still pay a ערך, but they do not pay דמים, because the dead have no worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: ערכין are stricter than נדרים in one way. How? If he said 'My ערך is upon me' and died, the heirs pay. If he said 'My דמים is upon me' and died, the heirs do not pay, because the dead have no worth.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives the other side: where ערכין are stricter. Its example is the death case from the משנה in step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערך is a fixed debt from the moment of the vow, so death does not cancel it. A vow of worth depends on the person's worth at the time it is valued, and a dead person has none. So on this point ערכין are harsher, which balances the two stricter points of נדרים in step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: "My ערך is upon me": a vow of the Torah's fixed amount
"My worth is upon me": a vow of one's market value
How so? (asking for an example)

steps.whatToRemember: Vows of worth are stricter in two ways: they apply to animals and birds, and there is no reduction for the poor. ערכין are stricter in one way: the heirs still pay after the pledger dies.

phrases.english: There is a stricter side to valuations than to vows. How so?
If he said: "My valuation is upon me," and died —
the heirs must give;
"My worth is upon me," and died —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second half of the same ברייתא. It gives the opposite side, using the same rule as the משנה in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ערכין are stricter in that the heirs must pay a ערך after the pledger dies, while דמים is not paid after death.

steps.title: Trying to prove that an oral loan is collected from heirs
steps.stepSummary: Since heirs pay a ערך that was pledged only by speech, the גמרא suggests that any מלוה על פה can be collected from heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said that if a person said 'my ערך is on me' and then died, his heirs pay. Can we learn from this that an oral loan is collected from heirs?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the ruling from Step 12 and tries to learn a general money-law rule from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערך pledge is only spoken, with no written document. Yet the heirs still pay it. So the גמרא suggests that any debt made only by speech, a מלוה על פה, should also be collectible from heirs.

keyTerms.meaning: A loan or debt made only by spoken words, with no document
Heirs

steps.title: A ערך is different because it is a debt written in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: a ערך is not an ordinary oral loan, because the Torah itself writes out the debt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is different, because a ערך is a debt written in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof from Step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amount of a ערך is fixed in the Torah by age and gender. So this debt is not 'only spoken.' It is written down in the Torah itself, and that is why heirs pay. Ordinary oral loans may still not be collected from heirs.

keyTerms.meaning: Here it is different

steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A ערך is not a plain oral debt, because its amount is written in the Torah.

steps.title: Trying to prove that a Torah debt counts like a document
steps.stepSummary: Building on that answer, the גמרא suggests that any debt written in the Torah counts like a debt written in a שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then learn from this: a debt written in the Torah is like a debt written in a document?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the answer from Step 14 and tries to learn a new general rule from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If heirs pay a ערך only because the Torah writes it out, then the Torah's writing works like a שטר. That would mean every Torah-based money obligation can be collected from heirs, just like a written loan.

keyTerms.meaning: A written document, such as a loan document
Is like, is considered the same as

phrases.english: Learn from this:
a loan that is written in the Torah
is considered like one written in a document?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: מִלְוָה הַכְּתוּבָה בַּתּוֹרָה כִּכְתוּבָה בִּשְׁטָר דָּמְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the previous answer into a new general conclusion.
steps.raayaObject: That a debt written in the Torah has the strength of a debt written in a document.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's ruling that heirs pay a ערך, as explained in Step 14.

steps.title: The ברייתא is a case where he already stood in court
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: the ברייתא is talking about a pledger who already stood in court and was ruled obligated before he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where he already stood in judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof from Step 15 by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before he died, the pledger was brought to בית דין and told to pay. A court ruling makes the debt as strong as a written one, so the heirs pay. The ברייתא therefore proves nothing about Torah debts in general.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? The גמרא is narrowing down the case
He stood in judgment: the court already ruled that he must pay

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here —
where he stood in judgment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof by limiting the ברייתא to a narrower case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects learning anything general about Torah debts from this ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The heirs pay because of the court ruling, not because the debt is written in the Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: This new case setup is exactly what the גמרא questions in the next step.

steps.title: Then why don't heirs pay דמים after a court ruling?
steps.stepSummary: If the ברייתא means he stood in court, the same should be true for דמים, so why don't the heirs pay there?
steps.simpleTranslation: In the matching case of 'my worth is on me,' where he also stood in judgment, why don't the heirs pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of Step 16 using the other half of the ברייתא, about דמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא puts the ערך case and the דמים case side by side. If the ערך case means he already stood in court, the דמים case should mean the same. A court ruling should make the heirs pay there too, but the ברייתא says they do not.

keyTerms.meaning: The matching case, the one just like it
'My worth is on me': a pledge to give one's market value
Why?

phrases.english: In the corresponding case of 'my worth is upon me'
where he stood in judgment,
why should the heirs not give for 'my worth is upon me'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'stood in court' answer by applying it to the דמים case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the ברייתא is about someone who stood in court.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both halves of the ברייתא should be read as the same case. A court ruling should then make heirs pay דמים too, which contradicts the ברייתא.

steps.title: דמים still needs a value estimate, while a ערך is fixed
steps.stepSummary: Even after a court ruling, דמים is missing an אומדנא of the person's value. A ערך has a fixed amount and is missing nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'My worth' is still missing an estimate. 'My ערך' is missing nothing at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of Step 17 by showing a real difference between the two pledges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With דמים, the court still has to estimate how much the person was worth, so the debt is not finished, and once he dies he can no longer be valued. With a ערך, the Torah sets the amount, so the court ruling settles everything and the heirs pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Still missing an estimate of the value
Not missing anything at all

steps.whatToRemember: Heirs pay a ערך because the pledger stood in court and the amount is fixed by the Torah. With דמים, the value estimate is still missing, so heirs do not pay.

phrases.english: It is lacking an assessment.
'My valuation is upon me' —
is not lacking anything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by pointing out how דמים and ערך differ.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A court ruling should work the same way for דמים and for ערך.
steps.terutzMaskana: A court ruling fully settles a ערך, which has a fixed amount. דמים still needs a value estimate, which cannot be done after death.

steps.title: רב: whoever pledges the ערך of a hand or leg still pays its worth
steps.stepSummary: Back to the משנה about pledging the ערך of a hand or leg: רב rules that the person still pays that limb's דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'The ערך of my hand or leg is on me'... רב גידל said in the name of רב: he gives its worth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to a line of the משנה and brings רב's added ruling on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said that pledging the ערך of a hand or leg means nothing, because ערכין apply only to a whole person. רב adds that he is not fully free: he must still pay what that limb is worth.

keyTerms.meaning: The ערך of my hand or my leg
And he gives its worth, meaning the value of that limb

steps.confusionAlert: רב's ruling does not fit the plain wording of the משנה, which says 'he has not said anything.' That is exactly what the גמרא challenges in the next step, and step 21 answers that the משנה follows the רבנן while רב follows רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: 'The valuation of my hand or leg is upon me,' etc.
Rav Giddel said that Rav said:
And he gives its worth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the heirs discussion and returns to a line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who pledges the ערך of a limb does not pay a ערך, but he must pay that limb's value.

steps.title: But the משנה says he said nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב: the משנה says that one who pledges the ערך of his hand or leg 'has not said anything,' so how can רב say he pays דמים?
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches that he 'has not said anything'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's ruling from Step 19. The משנה itself says this person's words mean nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said the person pays the דמים of the limb. But 'לא אמר כלום' sounds like a full exemption, with no ערך and no דמים. So רב seems to contradict the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: He has not said anything. His words create no obligation.
It teaches. Used when quoting what a משנה or ברייתא says.

phrases.english: But it teaches: 'he has not said anything'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling from the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that one who pledges the ערך of a limb pays its דמים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says 'he has not said anything,' which suggests no obligation at all, not even דמים.

steps.title: The משנה follows the רבנן, רב follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's 'he said nothing' follows the רבנן. רב's ruling that he pays דמים follows רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He has not said anything according to the רבנן, and he gives its דמים according to רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה and רב are following two different opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן say that if there is no ערך for a limb, the pledge is empty. רבי מאיר holds that a person does not speak for nothing. So when he said 'ערך' about something that has no ערך, he must have meant its דמים, its market value. רב rules like רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority opinion against רבי מאיר here.
Its value, meaning the market price of the limb.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up ערך and דמים. ערך is a fixed amount set by the Torah based on age and gender. דמים is what the person or limb would be worth if sold.

phrases.english: 'He has not said anything' is according to the Rabbis,
and 'he gives its value' is according to Rabbi Meir.
phrases.notes: רבי מאיר's view, taught earlier in the מסכתא, is that people don't say words for nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by splitting the opinions.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different opinions (the משנה follows one תנא, רב follows another).
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is the view of the רבנן, and רב rules like רבי מאיר, who holds that the person meant דמים.

steps.title: Didn't רב already say this about a vessel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב needed this ruling. He already taught that one who pledges the ערך of a vessel pays its דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he already said it once! For רב גידל said in the name of רב: One who says 'the ערך of this vessel is upon me' gives its דמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks why רב repeated himself. He already gave the same rule about a vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vessel has no ערך at all, just like a limb. רב already ruled that pledging a vessel's ערך means paying its דמים. So the limb ruling seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: One time. He already said it once.
A vessel or utensil, which has no ערך.
The fixed valuation the Torah sets for a person.

phrases.english: But he already said it once,
as Rav Giddel said that Rav said:
One who says: 'The valuation of this vessel is upon me'
gives its value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רב's ruling stands, the גמרא asks why it was needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for רב's ruling about a limb.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב already ruled the same about a vessel, so the limb ruling seems repetitive.

steps.title: With a limb we might think he simply made a mistake
steps.stepSummary: With a vessel, everyone knows there is no ערך, so he surely meant דמים. With a limb, he might have mistakenly thought a limb has a ערך like a head or liver. רב teaches that he still pays דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: there, a person knows a vessel has no ערך, so he decided and spoke in terms of דמים. But here, he made a mistake. He thought that just as there is 'the ערך of my head' and 'the ערך of my liver,' there is also 'the ערך of my hand' and 'the ערך of my leg,' and he did not mean דמים. So רב teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב needed both rulings. The limb case has a reason to exempt that the vessel case does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a vessel, the person knows a ערך is impossible, so his words must mean דמים. With a limb, he may honestly have thought a limb has its own ערך. Then he never meant דמים and should owe nothing. רב teaches that even so, we treat him as meaning דמים.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said. Introduces a mistaken idea the ruling comes to reject.
He is making a mistake.
He decided and spoke, meaning he spoke with clear intent.
It teaches us. The new point of the ruling.

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, following רבי מאיר, pledging the ערך of something that has no ערך means paying its דמים. This holds for a vessel, and it holds even for a limb, where he might have been confused.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
it is there that a person knows
that there is no valuation for a vessel,
so he decided and spoke for the sake of value,
but here he is making a mistake,
since he thinks that just as there is
'the valuation of my head' and 'the valuation of my liver,'
there is also 'the valuation of my hand' and 'the valuation of my leg,'
but he did not mean value —
so he teaches us that this is not so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'he already said it' challenge by showing a difference between the cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Both rulings are needed, because the limb case has a special reason to exempt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With a limb, the person mistakenly thought there was a ערך, so he never meant דמים and is exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with a limb, he is treated as meaning דמים and must pay.

steps.title: Why does pledging the head or liver mean the whole valuation?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: one who pledges the ערך of his head or liver gives his full ערך. It asks for the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The ערך of my head' or 'the ערך of my liver': he gives the ערך of his whole self. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and asks why it rules this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A hand or leg gives no ערך, yet a head or liver gives the full ערך of the whole person. The גמרא wants a source for this difference.

keyTerms.meaning: My liver.
The valuation of his entire self.
What is the reason?

phrases.english: 'The valuation of my head' or 'the valuation of my liver' —
he gives the valuation of his entire self.
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for why pledging the head or liver obligates the full ערך.

steps.title: The Torah speaks of 'lives'
steps.stepSummary: The Torah says ערכין is about 'נפשות,' lives. A head or liver is something a person's life depends on, so pledging it is like pledging the whole person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah says 'נפשות' (lives).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source: the פסוק about ערכין uses the word 'נפשות.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the Torah ties ערך to a person's life, a pledge on a part without which he cannot live counts as a pledge on his whole life. A hand or leg is different, because a person can live without them.

keyTerms.meaning: Lives or souls. The word used in the פסוק about ערכין.
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳.

steps.whatToRemember: A head or liver gives the full ערך, because a person's life depends on them and the Torah speaks of 'נפשות.' A hand or leg does not give a ערך.

phrases.english: The Merciful One says: 'lives.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Torah frames ערכין as 'נפשות,' so pledging a part a person's life depends on obligates the full ערך.

steps.title: The general rule includes the leg from the knee up
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's phrase 'זה הכלל' adds a case: pledging the ערך of one's leg from the knee and up obligates a full ערך.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'This is the rule: anything a person's life depends on...' The phrase is there to include a leg from the knee and above.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what extra case the משנה's words 'זה הכלל' come to include.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already listed the head and liver. 'זה הכלל' widens the rule to anything a person cannot live without. A leg cut off above the knee is fatal, so pledging its ערך is like pledging the whole person, and he pays a full ערך.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the general rule. It often comes to include more cases.
Something a person's life depends on
To include, meaning to bring in an extra case
Knee

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הַכְּלָל: דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ וכו׳.
phrases.english: This is the rule: anything a person's life depends on, etc.
This comes to include from the knee and above.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the reason given in step 25 (life depends on it) and extends it to a new case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pledging the ערך of one's leg from the knee upward obligates a full ערך, because a person cannot live without it.

steps.title: A dispute about pledging half of one's ערך
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא of a ברייתא says one who pledges 'half my ערך' pays half. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says he is 'לוקה' and pays a full ערך.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Half my ערך is on me' — he gives half. A ברייתא teaches: if someone says 'half my ערך is on me', he gives half his ערך. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says: he is lashed and gives a full ערך.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and brings a ברייתא where a תנא disagrees with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה and the תנא קמא treat 'half my ערך' simply: he promised half an amount, so he pays half. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה is much stricter. He requires a full ערך and even mentions 'lashes', which sounds very strange because nobody sinned here.

keyTerms.meaning: Half of my ערך, meaning half the money amount
Gets lashes, or more broadly, is punished
A full ערך

phrases.english: 'Half my ערך is upon me' — he gives, etc.
The Rabbis taught in a ברייתא:
'Half my ערך is upon me' — he gives half his ערך.
רבי יוסי son of רבי יהודה says:
He is lashed and gives a full ערך.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next case in the משנה: half of a ערך.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא says he pays half his ערך. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה says he is 'לוקה' and pays a full ערך.

steps.title: Why would he be lashed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה: this person did nothing wrong, so why would he get lashes?
steps.simpleTranslation: He is lashed?! Why?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised by the word 'לוקה' and challenges it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lashes are a punishment for breaking a prohibition. Making a vow to give half one's ערך to the בית המקדש is not a sin at all. So the word 'lashed' makes no sense if we read it literally.

keyTerms.meaning: Why?

phrases.english: He is lashed?! Why?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's statement in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's ruling that he is 'לוקה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Lashes are given only for a sin, and no sin was committed by pledging half a ערך.

steps.title: 'Lashed' means penalized by paying the full ערך
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that 'לוקה' means he is penalized by having to pay a full ערך. The reason is a rabbinic גזירה, so people won't confuse 'half my ערך' with 'the ערך of half of me'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: he is 'struck' with a full ערך. What is the reason? It is a decree: 'half his ערך' was made strict because of 'the ערך of half of him', and the ערך of half of him is something his life depends on.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge. 'Lashed' is not real lashes. It means a penalty: he must pay the full amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two cases that sound almost the same. 'The ערך of half of me' pledges half a body, which a person cannot live without, so by the Torah he pays a full ערך. 'Half my ערך' only means half the money. The חכמים worried people would mix them up, so they made 'half my ערך' cost a full ערך too.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made to protect against a mistake
Because of, out of concern for
The ערך of half of him, meaning half his body

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two phrases. 'חצי ערכי' (half my ערך) is about half the money. 'ערך חציי' (the ערך of half of me) is about half the body. Only the second is a full ערך by Torah law. The first is full only because of the גזירה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how a word like 'לוקה' can mean a money penalty, and how the חכמים protect a Torah rule by making a look-alike case strict too.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
He is 'struck' with a full ערך,
phrases.notes: 'Struck' here means he loses out by paying the whole amount. It doesn't mean lashes.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
It is a decree on 'half his ערך' because of 'the ערך of half of him',
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'ערכי' (my ערך), the word in round brackets. The corrected wording, in square brackets, is 'ערכו' (his ערך).

phrases.aramaic: וְעֵרֶךְ חֶצְיוֹ הָוֵי דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ.
phrases.english: and the ערך of half of him is something his life depends on.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לוֹקֶה בְּעֵרֶךְ שָׁלֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 28 by reading 'לוקה' as a money penalty.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word plus a rabbinic decree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'לוקה' means real lashes, which makes no sense when no sin was done.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'לוקה' means he is penalized by paying a full ערך. This is a גזירה so 'half my ערך' is not confused with 'the ערך of half of me'.

steps.title: Why does 'the דמים of half of me' cost the whole value?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about דמים: 'half my דמים' pays half, but 'the דמים of half of me' pays the full value. It asks for the reason, setting up the next answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Half my value is upon me' — he gives, etc. 'The value of half of me is upon me' — he gives the value of his whole self. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's דמים cases and asks why half a body costs the full value. This is setting up the next step, where the answer will come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With ערכין, the reason for paying in full was the Torah's word 'נפשות' (step 25). דמים is a different kind of pledge: it is the person's market value, and that word was not said about it. So why should half a body cost the full value here too?

keyTerms.meaning: My value, what I would sell for on the market
The value of half of me, meaning half my body
The value of his whole self

phrases.english: 'Half my value is upon me' — he gives, etc.
'The value of half of me is upon me' — he gives the value of his whole self,
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of the משנה, about דמים instead of ערכין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why pledging the דמים of half of oneself obligates the full value, since the 'נפשות' reasoning was said only about ערכין.

steps.title: A פסוק links pledges of value to ערך
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers why 'the דמים of half of me' obligates full value. The פסוק places the word נדר next to ערך, so the vital-organ rule of ערכין also applies to דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: 'a vow with your valuation of souls.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 30. It gives a פסוק as the source for why 'the דמים of half of me' obligates paying full value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק puts נדר (a pledge of value) right next to ערך (the Torah's fixed amount). This link teaches that the two work the same way. In ערכין, pledging a part the person cannot live without obligates the whole ערך, so the same is true for a pledge of דמים.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, a pledge to give a person's market value (דמים)
'With your valuation' — the Torah's fixed ערך amount
Souls, meaning living people
It is written (in a פסוק)

phrases.english: It is written: 'a vow with your valuation of souls.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 27:2. The word נדר sits right next to the word ערך, so the two are linked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does 'the דמים of half of me' obligate full value?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק links נדר to ערך, so pledging a vital part obligates the whole for דמים, just as it does for ערכין.

steps.title: The משנה's general rule adds the leg from the knee up
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's words 'זה הכלל — something life depends on' come to include pledging the value of one's leg from the knee and up.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: something the soul depends on. This comes to include from the knee and up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the משנה's phrase 'זה הכלל' adds. It includes a pledge of the leg from the knee and up, which also obligates the full value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person can die if the leg is cut off above the knee. That makes it a part 'the soul depends on', like the head or liver. The גמרא already made this point for ערכין in step 26, and here the same rule is applied to pledges of value now that step 31 has linked the two.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is the rule' — a phrase in a משנה that often adds more cases
The soul (life) depends on it, meaning a vital body part
To include (one more case)
Knee

phrases.english: This is the rule:
something the soul depends on —
this comes to include from the knee and up.
phrases.notes: He means someone who pledged the value of his leg from the knee up. He pays the value of his whole self.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the משנה's general rule to pledges of value, building on the link made in step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pledging the value of the leg from the knee and up counts as a vital part and obligates the full value.

steps.title: A ברייתא about pledging half the ערך of a utensil
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a מחלוקת about someone who pledges 'half the ערך of a כלי'. רבי מאיר says he pays its value, and the חכמים say his words mean nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: if someone pledges half the ערך of a utensil, רבי מאיר says he gives its value, and the חכמים say he has not said anything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא. Someone pledged 'half the ערך' of an object, even though objects have no ערך at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah sets ערך amounts only for people, so 'the ערך of a כלי' makes no literal sense. רבי מאיר reads the words as a pledge of the object's money value, so he pays half of it. The חכמים say the statement has no effect at all.

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes an ערך pledge
A utensil or object, which has no Torah ערך
Its money value
He has said nothing, meaning his words have no effect

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמַּעֲרִיךְ חֲצִי עֵרֶךְ כְּלִי,
phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: one who pledges half the valuation of a utensil —
רבי מאיר says: he gives its value,
phrases.notes: He means half of the object's value, matching the 'half' that was pledged.

phrases.english: and the חכמים say: he has not said anything.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמַּעֲרִיךְ חֲצִי עֵרֶךְ כְּלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: ערך language used for an object instead of a person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: pledging half the ערך of a כלי obligates half its value. חכמים: the pledge has no effect.

steps.title: At רבא's sickbed, רבי מאיר's reasoning is explained
steps.stepSummary: While visiting the sick רבא, אביי and other scholars explain רבי מאיר's view: a person does not speak for nothing. So the pledge means money, whether it was for the whole or for half.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא was sick, and אביי and other scholars went in to visit him. They sat and said: It makes sense that רבי מאיר holds a person does not speak words for nothing, so there is no difference between the whole and half.
steps.whatsHappening: In a story setting, the scholars explain why רבי מאיר's view is logical. This sets up their challenge against the חכמים in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds a basic principle: people do not say pointless things. Since 'the ערך of a כלי' cannot mean a real ערך, the person must have meant the object's value. This logic works the same for a whole pledge and a half pledge.

keyTerms.meaning: Became sick, weak
It makes sense that... (sets up a contrast with a view that is harder to explain)
A person does not say words for nothing (his words must mean something)
There is no difference

phrases.english: רבא became sick;
Abaye and other scholars went in to him,
and they were sitting and saying:
It makes sense for רבי מאיר — he holds
a person does not utter his words for nothing,

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא כּוּלּוֹ וְלָא שְׁנָא חֶצְיוֹ.
phrases.english: no difference whether the whole of it or half of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר קָסָבַר אֵין אָדָם מוֹצִיא דְּבָרָיו לְבַטָּלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רבי מאיר's view in the ברייתא, as setup for a challenge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר holds a person does not speak for nothing, so 'ערך of a כלי' means its value, whether whole or half.

steps.title: Challenge: the חכמים' view seems inconsistent
steps.stepSummary: The scholars ask what the חכמים hold. If words can be pointless, even a whole pledge should mean nothing. If words are never pointless, even a half pledge should count.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what do the חכמים hold? If a person does say words for nothing, then even the whole should mean nothing. And if a person does not say words for nothing, then even half should count!
steps.whatsHappening: The scholars challenge the חכמים with a two-sided question. Neither principle seems to explain why 'half the ערך of a כלי' means nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes the חכמים agree that a pledge of the whole ערך of a כלי obligates its value. So the only difference left is 'whole' versus 'half', and neither principle gives a reason to treat them differently. The challenge forces the גמרא to find a different explanation for the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: What do they hold? (what is their reasoning)
If... and if... — a two-sided challenge
Also, too

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never says the חכמים rule on a pledge of the whole ערך of a כלי. The challenge assumes they agree it obligates the value, and only argue about half.

phrases.english: But the חכמים — what do they hold?
If a person does utter his words for nothing —
then even the whole of it too!
phrases.notes: Meaning: then even someone who pledged the full ערך of an object should owe nothing.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אֵין אָדָם מוֹצִיא דְּבָרָיו לְבַטָּלָה —
phrases.english: And if a person does not utter his words for nothing —
then even half of it too!
phrases.notes: Meaning: then someone who pledged half should pay half the value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the חכמים with רבי מאיר, whose logic was just explained in step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of the חכמים that pledging half the ערך of a כלי means nothing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A two-sided challenge: either words can be pointless, so the whole should mean nothing too, or words are never pointless, so half should count too. Neither principle explains treating whole and half differently.

steps.title: The חכמים agree with both רבי מאיר and רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: רבא and אביי answer that the חכמים hold like רבי מאיר and also like רבי שמעון. Like רבי מאיר, they agree that a person does not say words for nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא and אביי said to them: The חכמים here hold like רבי מאיר, and they also hold like רבי שמעון. They hold like רבי מאיר, who said, 'A person does not say his words for nothing.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא and אביי begin answering the question from Step 35. They say the חכמים are not using one rule only. They combine two ideas.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 35 asked how the חכמים can treat a whole pledge as money but a half pledge as nothing. The answer is that the חכמים accept רבי מאיר's rule that words are not pointless. That is why a whole pledge becomes a money pledge. The second idea, from רבי שמעון, is explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים here, in this ברייתא
They hold, they agree with
A person does not say his words for nothing

phrases.english: Rava and Abaye said to them:

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּנַן דְּהָכָא כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבְרִי לַהּ,
phrases.english: The Rabbis here hold like Rabbi Meir,
and they hold like Rabbi Shimon.
They hold like Rabbi Meir, who said:
"A person does not say his words for nothing."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רָבָא וְאַבָּיֵי: רַבָּנַן דְּהָכָא כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר סָבְרִי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the חכמים's view raised in Step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The חכמים combine two different principles, one from רבי מאיר and one from רבי שמעון.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The חכמים must hold either that words can be pointless or that they never are, so their split ruling seems inconsistent.
steps.terutzMaskana: They accept רבי מאיר's rule that words are not pointless, together with רבי שמעון's rule, explained in the next step.

steps.title: Like רבי שמעון: nobody donates half a כלי
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים also follow רבי שמעון, who rules that an unusual kind of donation does not count. Donating a whole כלי is normal. Donating half of one is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: They also hold like רבי שמעון, who said a person is exempt because he did not donate the way people normally donate. Donating a whole item is the normal way. Donating half is not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא and אביי finish their answer by explaining the second idea, which comes from רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון holds that a pledge made in an odd, unusual way creates no duty at all. People commonly pledge a whole כלי, so רבי מאיר's rule applies and it counts as a money pledge. Nobody normally pledges half a כלי, so רבי שמעון's rule cancels that pledge. This explains why the חכמים say a half pledge is meaningless.

keyTerms.meaning: In the normal way people donate
Its normal way, how it is usually done
All of it, the whole thing
Half of it

steps.whatToRemember: The חכמים use two rules together. Words are not pointless, so a whole pledge counts as money. A pledge made in an unusual way does not count, so a half pledge is void.

phrases.english: And they hold like Rabbi Shimon,
who said that he did not donate
phrases.notes: This points to רבי שמעון's ruling elsewhere about pledging an offering in an odd way, like a מנחה of barley. There the person owes nothing.

phrases.english: in the way people donate;
a whole one is the normal way to donate,
half of one is not the normal way to donate.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְסָבְרִי לַהּ כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, דְּאָמַר שֶׁלֹּא הִתְנַדֵּב כְּדֶרֶךְ הַמִּתְנַדְּבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-part answer begun in Step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings in a second principle that limits the first.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If words are never pointless, a half pledge should also count as money.
steps.terutzMaskana: A half pledge is unusual. Under רבי שמעון's rule, an unusual pledge does not count, so it is void.

steps.title: Which case does the משנה mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about someone who pledged another person's ערך and then died. It asks what exact case this is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: someone who says, 'The ערך of so-and-so is upon me,' and the one who vowed dies, and so on. What case is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה. It quotes the line and asks what situation it describes, setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the heirs must pay. The גמרא wants to know when this is true, because a ערך is not always a settled debt at the moment the pledger dies.

keyTerms.meaning: The person who made the vow
What is it? Which case is meant?

phrases.english: One who says, "The valuation of so-and-so is upon me,"
and the one who vowed dies, etc.
What case is this?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאוֹמֵר ״עֶרְכּוֹ שֶׁל פְּלוֹנִי עָלַי״, וּמֵת הַנּוֹדֵר כּוּ׳. מַאי נִיהוּ?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion about half a כלי ends.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Under what conditions must the heirs pay the ערך of the other person?

steps.title: He had already stood in judgment
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the pledger already 'stood in judgment' before he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where he already stood in judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה means a case where the pledger stood in judgment before he died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the pledger has stood in judgment and the amount has been fixed, the pledge becomes a settled debt. A settled debt is passed on to the heirs, so they must pay it.

keyTerms.meaning: Stood in judgment, so the obligation was fixed before death

phrases.english: Where he stood in judgment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 38.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה refers to a pledger who stood in judgment before he died.

steps.title: Isn't this the same as the earlier clause?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that this clause now teaches the same thing as an earlier clause of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the same as that!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה for seeming to repeat itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier clause, about someone who says 'my ערך is upon me' and then dies, also says the heirs pay, and it was also explained as a case of standing in judgment. If both clauses mean the same case and the same rule, why does the משנה need this one?

keyTerms.meaning: This is the same as that, a complaint that something is repeated

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a challenge to the rule itself. The גמרא only asks why the משנה states the same rule twice.

phrases.english: This is the same as that!
phrases.notes: 'That' is the earlier clause about pledging 'my own ערך' and then dying. There too the heirs pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation in Step 39 because it makes the clause repeat an earlier one.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for this clause in the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both clauses refer to one who stood in judgment, the second clause adds nothing new.

steps.title: The clause was needed for its last part, about דמים
steps.stepSummary: The clause was repeated in order to teach its last part: if someone pledged another person's דמים and then died, the heirs must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed for the last part: 'The דמים of so-and-so is upon him, and the one who vowed dies, the heirs must give.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the repeated wording sets up the new case at the end of the clause, a pledge of someone's דמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The part about ערך only restates what we already knew. It is there to lead into the new case, pledging another person's דמים, which the earlier clause did not cover. The משנה states that in this case too, the heirs pay.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a משנה or a clause
It was needed
His value, what he would sell for
Heirs

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common way the גמרא handles repetition in a משנה. A line that seems repeated may be there only to lead into a new case that follows.

phrases.english: It was needed for the last part:
the value of so-and-so is upon him,
and the one who vowed dies,
the heirs must give.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 40 about repetition.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The repeated words exist to set up a new case at the end of the clause.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clause about another person's ערך seems to add nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is there to introduce the new case of pledging another person's דמים, where the heirs also pay.
